subject: northern clingfish
title: A Tide Pool Fish Holds 230 Times Its Weight Where Suction Cups Slip

scenes.text: This fish grips rock harder than any suction cup.
The northern clingfish, a hand-sized fish from Pacific tide pools, where every wave hits like a car crash.
Its belly fins are fused into one sucker. In lab tests it held 80 to 230 times its own body weight before letting go.
Man-made suction cups fail on rough or slimy rock. The clingfish held just as hard on surfaces as rough as sandpaper.
The edge of its sucker carries thousands of microscopic hair-like structures that mold into every bump and seal the gap.
Engineers are copying it for grippers that work wet and dirty. Now watch a wave try to move it.

description:
A small tide pool fish out-grips every suction cup ever made.
The northern clingfish of the Pacific Northwest has pelvic fins fused into an adhesive disc. In 2013 University of Washington researchers measured it holding 80 to 230 times its body weight, and it kept its grip on rough, slimy surfaces where commercial suction cups let go. The secret is a rim of tiny hair-like structures that conform to the surface and seal it. Engineers are studying it for better suction devices.
Which small animal has the most ridiculous strength for its size?
first_comment: The sucker works even on surfaces coated in algae slime, which is where octopus suckers and rubber cups both fail. What should engineers copy from nature next?
